rhetoric

RET-uh-rik -- stress on the first syllable, RET. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Rhetoric is the art of using language effectively and persuasively.

The debate team's coach drilled them in rhetoric, teaching exactly when a pause persuades more than a shout.

Example

The famous speech is a masterclass in rhetoric: the same ringing phrase returns again and again, each repetition building until the vast crowd is moved as one.

Repetition, rhythm, and imagery are deliberately arranged to move an audience -- language used as a craft. Notice the word is uncountable: we say 'a command of rhetoric,' never 'a rhetoric.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

eloquence: Eloquence is the quality of beautiful, moving, forceful expression -- we admire a speaker's eloquence. Rhetoric is the art and technique behind such effects: you can study rhetoric and list its devices, while eloquence is the polish an audience admires in the finished speech or page.

diction: Diction is a writer's or speaker's choice of words -- formal diction, plain diction. It names one ingredient of good writing. Rhetoric is the whole art of using language persuasively, arranging many tools at once, and word choice is only one of them.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

bluntness: plain, direct speech without adornment

inarticulateness: inability to express oneself clearly

Where it sits · how much deliberate craft is involved

persuasion → rhetoric → oratory

persuasion vs. rhetoric: Persuasion is the broader, plainer word -- any nudge that changes a mind counts, while rhetoric names the studied art behind it: the deliberate craft of choosing words that move an audience.

oratory vs. rhetoric: Oratory is rhetoric at full ceremony: rhetoric is the art of effective language wherever it appears, even on the page, while oratory is that art performed aloud -- the grand public speech delivered from the podium.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — rhetor: public speaker, orator (Greek)

suffix — -ic: having the characteristics of; like (Greek -ikos, via Latin -icus)

Put it together: Remember the lead card's False Friends warning? Rhetoric is one of its two named examples (along with intrinsic). The word comes from Greek rhetorike tekhne, 'the art of the orator,' from rhetor, 'public speaker' -- but it arrived in English as one whole piece. Unlike caustic or aromatic, there was never an English base word that took on -ic; the ending here is a surface look-alike, not a suffix you can peel off. The meaning still honors its root: rhetoric is the orator's art.

Use the root in a new word: rhetorician: The debate coach was a skilled rhetorician who could argue almost any side of an issue.

Word Building

Word Choice

Rhetoric is a mass noun -- never 'a rhetoric' or 'rhetorics.' Say 'empty rhetoric,' 'the senator's rhetoric,' or 'a piece of political rhetoric' (where 'piece of' does the counting). It can be neutral praise for the art of persuasion or a jab at style without substance, as in 'all rhetoric, no plan.'
